items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.
Roman Catholic parishes fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Scranton was erected in 1868; sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: Federal census records (1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900) are the most direct and accessible source for identifying children living in the John Doyle/Bridget Halloran household in Schuylkill County. Each census captures a household snapshot, and together the five decennial censuses cover the entire period when children of this couple would be growing up at home. FamilySearch has all five years fully indexed and free. Search under 'John Doyle' + Schuylkill County, then under 'Bridget Halloran' / 'Bridget Doyle' for years after John's likely death. Try variant spellings: Doyl, Doy; Halloran, Haloron, Haloran, Halorn.

Pennsylvania civil birth registration did not begin until 1906; baptismal registers are therefore the primary birth record for any children of Bridget Halloran and John Doyle. The FamilySearch collection 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708-1985, ~982K indexed persons) includes Roman Catholic parish registers for the anthracite-coal Irish community — St. Patrick's (Pottsville) and neighboring parishes — which fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia until 1868, then the Diocese of Scranton. Search under father 'John Doyle' with mother 'Bridget Halloran.' Per the locality quirk, some films for this region are browse-only image groups; if indexed search yields nothing, plan to browse the relevant parish volumes.

If John Doyle died in Schuylkill County and left a will or letters of administration, it would be filed with the county Register of Wills (records survive from 1811). A will directly names all surviving children as heirs — the most authoritative single list of children. The FamilySearch collection 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994' (collection 1999196) covers Schuylkill County with 2.3M images. Note: personCount=0 in the collection metadata indicates this is a browse-only image collection, not name-indexed. Search the county Orphans' Court docket index (available at the Schuylkill County courthouse or on microfilm) to locate the volume/page, then read the image. Date window set by John Doyle's plausible lifespan as the record creator: he fathered children with Bridget beginning ca. 1838 and could have died anywhere from then to ca. 1910.

FAN item — Ellen Doyle is the one child of Bridget Halloran and John Doyle already identified. Her own later records are the most likely to name siblings directly: a Pennsylvania death certificate (available from 1906) names an informant who often lists immediate family; a marriage record would supply her father's name confirming parentage; an obituary would list surviving siblings. Search FamilySearch indexed vital records for 'Ellen Doyle' in Pennsylvania. Date window set by Ellen's plausible lifespan: born ca. 1838-1865 (when her parents were together in Schuylkill County), died plausibly 1880-1940.

Obituaries in Schuylkill County newspapers — especially the Miners' Journal (Pottsville, 1825-present), the region's paper of record — routinely listed surviving children by name. Search for John Doyle's death notice and Bridget Halloran's obituary (and any obituary under her remarried surname). Free access via Chronicling America (Library of Congress digitized newspapers); subscription access via Newspapers.com and GenealogyBank for additional coverage. A surviving-children list in either obituary would provide a near-complete roster of the Doyle children. Try variant spellings and both spouses' names.

Family burial plots cluster household members, and a family monument may list multiple children — including those who died in infancy and therefore never appeared in a census. Search FindAGrave and BillionGraves for John Doyle and Bridget Halloran in Schuylkill County; then inspect adjacent burials and the same plot for infant and child Doyle burials. Children who died young before any census are otherwise invisible to the research but would appear here. FindAGrave has extensive Schuylkill County coverage from community volunteer memorials.

The question refers to John Doyle as Bridget's 'first husband,' implying she remarried. Bridget's second marriage record serves two purposes: (a) it verifies the 'first husband' characterization and supplies the approximate date of John Doyle's death or the end of their union, anchoring the date range for children who could be his; and (b) any later household census under the second husband's name would capture Doyle children still living at home — but only if we know the second surname. Ancestry holds Pennsylvania marriage records, county marriage licenses, and bonds; also check FamilySearch for a free parallel search. Date window set by Bridget's plausible remarriage window: after John Doyle's death and before ca. 1910.

Fallback for plan item 1 (FamilySearch census search). The FamilySearch-curated external links specifically list '1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County' on Ancestry (collection 1276). Ancestry's 1850 census index uses independent transcriptions that may capture name variants missed by FamilySearch's index. If item 1 returns no Doyle household in the 1850 census, try Ancestry's dedicated Schuylkill County 1850 collection with broader name matching.
